title: Data structures and algorithms
summary: Learn how a data structure keeps items and an algorithm uses clear steps. Add three scores with the same small program in six languages.
introduction: A school bag holds your books. A packing plan tells you what to put in it first. Programs also need a way to hold things and a plan for working with them. This tutorial teaches both ideas with tiny examples you can check by hand.
learningObjectives: Explain the words data structure and algorithm
Trace a running total one step at a time
Choose one language for the tutorial

blocks.text: **Data** means facts, such as scores or names. A **data structure** is a way to keep those facts. An array keeps items in numbered places, like seats in a row.
An **algorithm** is a clear set of steps that finishes a task. A recipe is an everyday example. The steps must say what to do, in what order, and when to stop.

DSA is short for data structures and algorithms. It helps us find, sort, count, and connect information. It is not a programming language or a tool for drawing a web page. You write these ideas using a language.
Start with one language you know. If you are new to all six, JavaScript lets you try the examples in this site. You can compare the other tabs later. You do not need to learn all six at once.

items: Keep the scores 4, 7, and 2 in an array.
Start a running total at 0. A running total is the sum so far.
Add 4 to get 4. Add 7 to get 11. Add 2 to get 13.
Stop after the last score and print 13.

blocks.text: Choose one tab. All six programs do the same task and print the same result. JavaScript can run here. The other languages need the separate local tools in [Language setup](/tutorials/data-structures-algorithms/language-setup).

variants.caption: Run this JavaScript in the browser playground, or save main.js and use Node.js.
Use a separate local C11 compiler. Save this complete program as main.c; see Language setup.
Use a separate local C++17 compiler. Save this complete program as main.cpp; see Language setup.

variants.code:
scores = [4, 7, 2]
total = 0
for score in scores:
    total += score
print(total)
variants.caption: Use a separate local Python 3 interpreter. Save this complete program as main.py; see Language setup.
Use a separate local .NET 8 or newer console project. Replace Program.cs with this complete program.
Use a separate local JDK 17 or newer. Save this complete program as Main.java; see Language setup.

blocks.text: The array is the data structure. Starting at zero, visiting each score, and adding it is the algorithm. A loop repeats a step. The loop here visits each score once.
Check the small and tricky cases
For no scores, the total should stay 0. For one score, the total should equal that score. These are **edge cases**: small or unusual inputs that still need a correct answer.
Our numbers are small. Number limits differ between languages. Fixed-size integer types can run out of room for huge totals. We use small whole numbers so the idea stays clear.

items: Change the last score from 2 to 5. Work out the new total before running the code.
You should get 16: 4 + 7 + 5 = 16. The steps stay the same even though one value changed.

blocks.title: A common mistake
blocks.text: Keep the line that starts total at 0 before the loop. If you reset the total inside the loop, you throw away the sum of earlier scores.
